item.title: What Does It Actually Mean to Write ‘Like a Human’?
item.description:
<![CDATA[
What does it mean to write with a “human touch”? That’s what Marcus Olang’, a writer in Nairobi, Kenya, wondered after he was told a project proposal he worked on for days sounded as if it was written by ChatGPT. He explains how the massive effort to crack down on A.I. writing hides a deeper story. It’s not actually about technology, but how fluid and fraught the definition of sounding — being — human has always been.

item.title: Bringing More Women Into the Pulpit — and the Classroom
item.description:
To the Rev. Dr. Lisa L. Thompson, the 17th president of Union Theological Seminary, medical doctors, legal clerks and climate activists can gain as much from the storied New York institution she leads as aspiring faith leaders do.

Since taking the helm of Union in July, Dr. Thompson, 44, who at onetime was an assistant professor there, has aimed to expand what she calls the university’s “borderless” education style.

“The surgeon who’s about to perform surgery, I want them to think about what choices they’re making and why they’re about to make those choices,” she said. “And the implications of those choices on the human life that’s on the table in front of them.”

It is an approach in keeping with the university’s longstanding mission of education for social justice and theology. The flags outside Burke Library, the university’s main building, bear the phrase, “Blessed are the activists.”

And it’s fitting for the current moment, as a new crop of elected officials and political organizers have given religious Democrats a new face. Dr. Thompson said she was heartened to watch the political rise of a handful of theologians, including James Talarico of Texas, who studied at a seminary in the state before running for office. He will join Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia in the U.S. Senate, a fellow Democrat who is a pastor and who received both his master’s and doctoral degrees from Union.

But Dr. Thompson still sees work to be done in her position as Union’s first Black and only second woman leader. The daughter of working-class landowners from North Carolina, she has focused her studies on the relationship between race, gender and faith. She hopes her leadership expands both her university’s and the broader public’s understanding of how religion functions in everyday life.

We sat down with Dr. Thompson on Union’s campus shortly after her first four months as president. The conversation has been edited and condensed.

The tradition of faith leaders pursuing politics is nothing new. But more people are paying attention to it. Why do you think that is?

Christianity is not one thing, so I think that’s what we’re actually seeing. And this time, there’s a way to just say, our values are lived out in many different ways, and more players are coming into a greater spotlight in that conversation to help shape it, and to show how they’ve been working behind the scenes all along.

Not a lot of female theologians in politics though.

You want to talk about women and leadership? And how patriarchy is an equal-opportunity employer? My work often studies the influence of society on religion. This is a relationship that talks back to one another. You don’t go into a community of faith that is not shaped by the external social problems and social realities. On the same side, you do not step into society without having the influence of religion. And one of those influences is patriarchy and sexism, which are still real, live issues and problems in our midst.

What perspective do you bring to Union as its first Black president — its first Black woman president? And how are you viewing your responsibility through a theological lens?

If you want to take a Black feminist theological lens, what that means for me is the commitment to the social, political, and spiritual freedom, and economic freedom of women, and also how that impacts all people. There is something about starting with those who know a particular way of living and being in society.

So for me, that’s more about method: When I think about my scholarship, that’s a method. When I think about the leadership, that means that’s a method of my leadership. That means I’m thinking about how do we hire? Who are we hiring? Who has access to our education? I want to know how people get access to higher education, theological education, who will never get a degree.

What’s the conversation like right now among women who are university presidents or women in academic leadership? What are you hearing the most?

How do you break open the expectations of even how people expect you to dress? How they expect you to speak, how they expect you to show up with authority or not? All those are things that women in leadership right now, especially in higher education, are talking about. You’re still facing boards and institutions that are predominantly male. Those are matters that we face and how that impacts our engagement and decision-making. Those are the conversations that were on the table then and they’re active in live conversations now.

The other thing that’s on the table often is, where do you find community? One of the refrains people keep telling me is, “It’s lonely at the top.”

Where do you find community?

Oh, that’s hard right now. I still take my family, my friends. My social days are still important to me. But also, I think every level of elevation requires networking. I’m in a phase now, especially with this leadership move, where I’ve had to look to leaders of other organizations who have similar roles, but maybe in a different way. But it takes initiating those conversations.

]]>

item.title: Notable Books
item.description:
Good morning! Want to add a new book to your 2026 reading list? It’s not too late.

Our list of the 100 most notable books of the year just dropped, and I’m eager to get reading. I’ve been slacking this year (mainly because I’ve been reading a lot of news), but I did finish “Yesteryear” by Caro Claire Burke.

Not sure where to start? Use our guide. The categories will help you match the vibe you’re looking for. I’m going to read “Lost Lambs” by Madeline Cash next, which my friend Morgan lent to me. What books have you loved this year? Tell me.

We’re also covering:

Jensen Huang

The new Labubu?

Thanksgiving tips

What to discuss in class today.

1. President Trump pushed for Jensen Huang to be reinstated as chief executive of Nvidia. Trump set in motion a weekend of maneuvering, led by Vice President JD Vance, to get Huang his job back. Here’s how he did it.

2. The Army is moving ahead with plans to blow up a stockpile of explosives in Iowa tomorrow. It threatens to send a cloud of toxic lead dust over homes and farmland.

3. Representative Jimmy Gomez of California said that he would resign from Congress. A House committee had found that he had engaged in “unwelcome sexual conduct” with a female congressional aide.

4. More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war with Ukraine, according to a new estimate from hacked government data.

5. Some Haitian families fleeing to Canada are being separated at the border. Many are being denied entry, turned back and detained by U.S. authorities.

6. What’s in those drugs at gas station convenience stores and smoke shops? We tested some to find out.

What you’re wearing.

Cindy Phan, 20, neuroscience major at the University of Alabama

The outfit: My friends and I celebrated the upcoming release of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” by having a “Hunger Games”-themed Friendsgiving costume party! My outfit is roughly based on Effie Trinket’s monarch butterfly look (on a budget and rushed time frame). It was an absolute blast. Don’t forget, “eyes bright, chins up, smiles on!”

Tell me more! I love hosting hangouts with my friends, and having a themed party is my absolute favorite. I think college students should bring back embracing our inner child and live a life full of whimsy, not caring what other people think. There are more ways to have fun in college than just going out to the bars!

Submit your outfits to Fit Check.

I’m now obsessed with Ralphie VII, the University of Colorado’s live buffalo mascot. The previous Ralphie, known as Ralphie VI, retired because of her “indifference to running.”

The Make America Great Again movement wants to remake Harvard. Now Harvard has a class for that. See what was on the syllabus.

Walter Willett, a nutritionist at Harvard, studies the link between diet and health, which is a high priority for Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. His grants were frozen anyway.

A freshman at Stanford University was arrested after allegedly hacking into on-campus businesses and stealing funds. (The Stanford Daily)

The University of Minnesota announced its plan to close six residential communities designed to serve specific cultural groups in its dorms. Four of the communities were under scrutiny from the federal government. (The Minnesota Daily)

The new Labubu? Meet the Mirumi. The robotic bag charm can grab onto your bag and turn its head at the sound of your voice. My colleague Alisha Haridasani Gupta, who wrote this story, showed me the Mirumi in the newsroom. I need one.

Would you bid on live lobsters? It’s possible on Whatnot, a livestream auction app that is a cross between eBay and Twitch. You can also buy king crab legs, Wagyu hot dogs and ground beef.

Miley Cyrus got married. She married her partner of several years, Maxx Morando, at Frank Sinatra’s estate in Palm Springs, Calif.

Do these to get ahead for Thanksgiving!

Eat for pleasure. Savoring food for pleasure isn’t exclusively for the holidays. It may have long-term benefits.

Travel smart (and safe). If the recent outages have made you nervous, consult our Thanksgiving travel guide.

Looking for more things to read en route? Peruse some Thanksgiving-themed literature.

Don’t go to the emergency room. Avoid Thanksgiving hazards with these tips. Please, please don’t deep-fry a frozen turkey!

We want to know what you talk about at the Thanksgiving table. Tell us all about it here.

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. We’re taking the rest of the week off for the holiday. We’ll see you Monday!

This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U.S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

Forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T.A.

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that includes top headlines and analysis.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes.com.

The editor of Extra Credit is Talya Minsberg. Philip Pacheco and Hiroko Masuike were our photo editors.

]]>

item.title: Jensen Huang’s Startling Comeback at Nvidia
item.description:
To the Editor:

Re “Nvidia Reinstates Huang as Its C.E.O. at Trump’s Urging” (front page, Nov. 24):

While President Trump, tech traders and Wall Street investors are celebrating Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as its chief executive, the fact remains that he engaged in a reckless affair that could have compromised U.S. national security.

There is something especially troubling about the president’s nonchalant attitude in light of U.S. intelligence reports indicating that Alice Huang, with whom Mr. Huang had an affair, was in regular contact with an officer in China’s top spy agency.

The decision by a profit-driven corporate board to put Mr. Huang back in the driver’s seat at the world’s leading maker of advanced A.I. chips appears shortsighted and dismissive of the longer term message it sends to the world about our priorities.

Cody LyonBrooklyn

To the Editor:

The reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s chief executive is a declaration of moral bankruptcy by its board of directors.

Here is man who apparently circumvented American export controls to allow advanced Nvidia chips to reach China through Asian intermediaries, who has admitted to extramarital infidelity and who had intimate relationships with both a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence and another who is a company employee. He has also placed family members in influential corporate positions.

Yet without even waiting for its own investigation to conclude, the board has apparently decided that Mr. Huang’s commercial value outweighs every other consideration. In doing so, it has placed a dollar value on integrity — and found it expendable.

Mervyn TurnerScotch Plains, N.J.

To the Editor:

Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia raises two questions.

First, how can Nvidia’s employees, including Mr. Huang, hold security clearances while his involvement with Alice Huang and her former company Megaspeed, and Alibaba and perhaps other companies, is still being investigated?

Second, what steps have the U.S. defense and intelligence communities taken to determine if Nvidia chips installed in U.S. systems have hidden capabilities to capture and transmit their activities to unauthorized third parties?

President Trump, in the face of explicit warnings from the intelligence community and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is compromising our national security. This raises constitutional questions. Is this Congress, still controlled by conservatives, paying attention?

Kai LeeIndianapolis

To the Editor:

Just when I thought an American company had shown some spine and some respect for values other than shareholder value, Jensen Huang was returned to his position as head of Nvidia. Somehow, I had believed that the recent front-page New York Times story about his being an awful boss had defeated him for good.

Mr. Huang’s reinstatement is a metaphor for the utterly amoral excesses of our present capitalist, shareholder-value-driven-to-the-exclusion-of-all-else system.

I am embarrassed for having been so naïve as to think it might have been otherwise.

David E. Van IderstineLos Angeles

To the Editor:

Re “Texas Prisoner Screamed in Pain as Drugs Flowed During Execution, Witnesses Say” (news article, Nov. 21):

A great nation does not execute its citizens.

A great nation does not cause or perpetuate suffering.

A great nation does not allow an unequal application of justice.

Capital punishment is barbaric and inhumane and should be abolished.

We can, and must, be better.

John ButlerHuntingdon Valley, Pa.

To the Editor:

Re “Dear American Parent: You’re Welcome!,” by Jennifer L. Jennings (Opinion guest essay, Nov. 8):

Professor Jennings’s essay made me laugh. As a mother of three in Idaho, I’ve spent months navigating the maze of school choice, and I can assure you, the options are plentiful. The answers? Not so much.

I researched public schools, charter schools, online academies and everything in between. There were applications, assessments, tuition quotes that made me question whether I was enrolling my children in school or purchasing a second home, and enough Zoom calls to earn another degree.

But beneath all that frustration was a simple concern: Were my children being challenged enough in public schools?

This month, I finally enrolled my two older sons in an online school. So far, we’re loving it. Ask me again in six months.

School choice isn’t just about having more options. It’s about finding an education that fits the child, rather than expecting every child to fit the same system.

Nida MannanPocatello, Idaho

]]>

item.title: Virginia School District Shaken by Sex Abuse Claims Closes for a Week
item.description:
Just as classes were ending on Wednesday afternoon, parents in the Charlottesville, Va., area received unsettling news: All schools in the district would be shut down until after Thanksgiving.

The district had discovered that more than 500 employees had not received proper background checks, the announcement said. For the safety of the district’s 14,000 students, schools would stay closed until the employees had been vetted.

Employees hired in the past three years had received criminal background checks, the school district said. But they had not been checked against the state’s registry of child abuse complaints, which Virginia law requires.

The closure is the latest problem faced this year by the Albemarle County school district, which has been engulfed in a crisis triggered by child sex abuse allegations against an elementary school social emotional learning coach.

Since those allegations came to light at the beginning of 2026, three administrators have been charged with failure to report child abuse, the superintendent and three school board members have resigned and a prosecutor questioned the district’s “trustworthiness” in court.

In early October, the governor, Abigail Spanberger, called on law enforcement to “indict, charge, prosecute every single person who failed to do their job.”

Parents have been left with deep concerns even as they scramble to manage five unexpected days off before the Thanksgiving holiday break.

“I’m not worried about taking off work,” said Tyler Zimmerman, a father of a kindergarten student. “I’m more worried about what we’re sending them into.”

Mr. Zimmerman’s wife, Kalie, echoed a frequent complaint that the school district had been less than forthcoming about the sex abuse case and the systemic problems it had exposed.

“We found out from the media before we found out from the school. We had to find out from Facebook,” she said, adding, “Give us some answers.”

On Friday, Albemarle County Public Schools did not immediately respond to questions and the school board president did not respond to an interview request.

“The Albemarle County School Board fully understands the gravity of the current situation,” the board’s president, Rebecca Berlin, said in a statement in October, adding, “For too long, the school division has failed to invest in the essential systems and infrastructure necessary to be responsive to the needs of a school division our size.”

She also said that the board would not comment on ongoing criminal cases.

The crisis began when a student reported that a social emotional coach who had been assigned to two elementary schools, Woodbrook and then Hollymead, had touched her inappropriately.

The coach, Michael J. Swiney, was placed on leave in January, and a police investigation identified three more suspected victims, with reports of unwanted contact between August 2024 and January 2026.

While the investigation into Mr. Swiney was ongoing, a fifth-grade teacher at Woodbrook Elementary, Nicholas Clark, was arrested at the school on child pornography charges. Mr. Clark has since pleaded guilty.

In statements made before the lapses in the screening process were discovered, the district said that both Mr. Swiney and Mr. Clark had passed all required background checks. Mr. Swiney was hired in 2001, before the lapses were said to have begun; it is not clear when Mr. Clark was hired.

The problems at Hollymead were largely unknown to parents until June, when Mr. Swiney was indicted on 11 felony charges. Chris Leibig, who is representing Mr. Swiney, said on Sunday that he had no comment other than that his client would be pleading not guilty.

At a town hall meeting a few days after Mr. Swiney was indicted, parents expressed frustration that they could not find out if their children had ever met one-on-one with Mr. Swiney, whose job was to help students build social and emotional skills.

Parents also complained that the longtime school superintendent, Matt Haas, seemed unprepared to answer obvious questions.

Mr. Haas was forced to resign the next day, but the school board agreed to continue his salary and benefits for another year, complete with a raise and bonus, according to local news reports.

An assistant superintendent, Chandra Hayes, was appointed as interim superintendent.

As school officials fielded angry questions about who knew what and when, new problems arose.

In August, critics were frustrated when, in response to demands for an independent investigation, the school board tapped a law firm that was already representing the district in other cases.

In September, a first-term school board member, Jim Dillenbeck, held his own town hall meeting where he told parents that more than 15 staff members, including three principals, had been placed on administrative leave.

He complained of a practice of transferring problem employees, mentioning a specific transfer without naming names. A few days later, a teacher whose transfer fit the description died by suicide.

The board demanded Mr. Dillenbeck’s resignation, saying he had revealed confidential information and spread misinformation and rumors.

In an interview, Mr. Dillenbeck said he had agreed to resign because staying on the board would have been counterproductive. However, he defended the town hall.

“In my opinion,” he said, “I was serving the voters in my district who are desperate for honesty and transparency and student safety.”

Then in October, a grand jury indicted Mr. Swiney on additional charges, bringing the total number of suspected victims to seven.

Additional indictments came down against three administrators: the district’s Title IX coordinator, Erin Stone; the deputy chief of human resources, Jhonce Brodie Downs; and the former principal of Hollymead, Joe McCauley, who resigned after the scandal broke.

Each was charged with three counts of failing to report suspected child abuse.

Lawyers representing Ms. Stone and Mr. Downs declined to comment. Mr. McCauley’s lawyer, Elliott Bender, said his client would be pleading not guilty and would “vigorously fight to clear his name.”

The district said in June that it first learned about the allegations against Mr. Swiney in January.

But in a court hearing in August, a prosecutor said that in March 2025, the district had received a report about Mr. Swiney and had advised him to “keep his door open as much as possible in meeting with kids.” The indictments say the failure to report began as early as March 2025.

In addition, the police said that their investigation had shown that school district employees feared retaliation if they reported suspected child abuse.

On Oct. 29, the parents of a student with autism filed a federal lawsuit against the district, saying their child had been sexually assaulted by another student who was known to be “handsy,” and the district had done nothing.

The family further said that when it was time to renew their child’s individualized education plan, they were told they would first be required to sign an agreement releasing any claims against the district and promising not to disparage district employees.

The district has repeatedly declined to comment on ongoing legal matters.

All of this has led to a sense that the district’s culture needs an overhaul, several parents said in interviews. Morale has plummeted, there is still tremendous uncertainty about the district’s policy and actions, and in response to the crisis, it appears that employees are being placed on leave over minor concerns, parents said.

“Teachers don’t know if they can hug a child; they don’t know if they can hold the child’s hand if they’re crying,” said Christina Ha, a mother of three elementary school children and an officer of the district’s family council, an advocacy group made up of parents. “There has been a culture of fear and retaliation — there still is. That, as a parent, has been one of my biggest concerns.”

Ms. Ha and other parents expressed dismay that the school closure, though necessary, had come on the watch of Ms. Hayes, the acting superintendent, whom they praised for being more in touch with teachers and parents than her predecessor.

On Friday, the district posted a progress report on the background checks: 337 out of 524 employees had been checked against the registry, and all of them had been cleared.

Kirsten Luce contributed reporting.

]]>
